title: London police investigated after stopped cyclist dies
article: Five police officers in London, Ont., are under investigation by a provincial watchdog agency after a cyclist died in hospital on Tuesday, prompting a member of a group that protects riders' rights to say that attitudes toward them have changed little in recent years.
"And I'm not optimistic that the situation [between cyclists and police]is going to improve soon," said Ben Smith Lea of the Advocacy for Respect for Cyclists in Toronto.
Autopsy results revealed that Larry Campbell, 52, died of respiratory failure two weeks after he was stopped by police for committing an undisclosed infraction under the Highway Traffic Act.

According to a relative, Mr. Campbell had scrapes on his nose, chin and head, along with dark bruising under his lip. The relative added that he "looked like he had kissed the ground" and his spine was severely damaged, leaving him in a position where he would be unable to breathe on his own.

Gail Scala, a spokeswoman for the Special Investigations Unit, was unable to disclose more details about the London case because of the investigation, only adding that Mr. Campbell was treated for neck and head injuries.
In a news release issued after the arrest, London police said Mr. Campbell put up a struggle and "sustained an injury which required him to be transported to hospital for treatment."

Last week at a Critical Mass rally in Toronto, there was more tension between cyclists and police. Mr. Smith Lea said that police acted aggressively toward a cyclist who was later arrested for allegedly spitting on an officer.

"They very aggressively attacked him. They tackled him off his bike, then they put their knees on his head," Mr. Smith Lea said. "That's how they restrained him, even though he offered no resistance. He said they punched him after he was handcuffed."

The rally, an event typically held on the last Friday of each month, is a show of solidarity between cyclists, who parade up and down streets. But they slow traffic and can make "some motorists very angry," said an officer at Toronto's 52 Division.
Constable Brian Stacey, one of 50 officers at the division who patrol by bike, added that infractions by cyclists are going up.
Adding to many cyclists' frustrations is the fact that the city is trying to persuade residents to use their cars less often.
